title: Model-Informed Gold Revisions Inflate Measured Accuracy: A Versioned Gold-Standard Protocol for LLM Extraction of ESG Data
abstract: Language-model extraction of ESG data is scored against human references that are often revised after the model has run, yet those revisions are seldom versioned or measured. We propose a versioned gold-standard protocol: a blind reference fixed before extraction, every later revision logged with its page evidence and trigger, identical predictions scored against every version, and a worst-case headline. We apply it to 36 stratified Hang Seng Index constituents (396 cells, eleven headline fields). Revisions prompted by model disagreement change 22 cells, 21 toward the model, and raise measured accuracy by 5.1 percentage points with the predictions unchanged. Against the blind reference, a BM25-plus-LLM pipeline scores 90.9% (firm-bootstrap 95% CI 87.1-93.9%) on the 24 firms annotated fully blind and never used in prompt development, and 90.7% on all 36 (89.6% under the pre-specified unit normaliser). A generic regex-and-table heuristic scores 35.6%. Retrieval placed the gold evidence page in the model's context for 98% of disclosed cells, including every missed or wrong value that has a cited page. Under the written prompt, only two of the 37 errors are model errors, plus one masked by an identical gold error. The rest are gold omissions, prompt-gold specification conflicts, definitional ambiguity and unverifiable disclosure. For this reasoning model, residual error arises after retrieval, in the definition of the target; a partial comparison suggests a weaker model loses about ten points. ESG extraction accuracy is a property of a model and a reference together, and benchmarks should report both.
why: Versioned gold-standard protocol shows revisions inflate LLM extraction accuracy.

title: Market Impact Estimation via Causal Foundation Models
abstract: When a trader executes a large order, the relevant question is not \emph{what will the price be?} but \emph{what would the price have been had I not traded?} Market impact is thus a causal quantity, yet classical models (Almgren--Chriss, propagators) regress price on flow, which is biased whenever informed flow moves prices through information as well as trading. We present a proof-of-concept \emph{Causal Market Simulator}: a continuous-time causal prior-data fitted network (PFN) trained on a synthetic market prior in which a hidden informational flow confounds the flow--price relation by construction, with confounding strength an exact per-episode knob. On this prior, the naive estimator's bias follows a closed form we confirm empirically (up to 68\% overestimation), while the PFN tracks the unbiased true-parameter oracle at high confounding. Its \emph{do-ablated twin}, the same model with the intervention inputs removed, collapses onto the pre-window mean. Zero-shot, the model responds at the ground-truth scale to metaorders in an ABIDES limit-order book ($+0.38$ pre-onset standard deviations against seed-replay counterfactuals), and its intervention response replicates on about 2,300 detected flow bursts in BTC/ETH/SOL perpetuals and 3,800 on Nasdaq equities, evidence consistent with, though not proof of, causal transfer. Off-prior the response degrades gracefully, and split-conformal recalibration repairs interval calibration. Transfer hinges on encoding the metaorder as added flow rather than a clamped price level, not on more training. A recurrent state-space variant closes the remaining shape gap: its impact accrues over execution duration where the transformer's stays flat, raising the correlation with measured metaorder impact from $+0.68$ to between $+0.92$ and $+0.96$, at the cost of weaker on-prior deconfounding that traces to the training recipe rather than to recurrence.
why: Causal PFN for market impact with confounding; execution-relevant but proof-of-concept.

title: Do LLM Screeners Share a Template? Auditing Surface-Feature Preferences in AI Resume and Loan Screening
abstract: When large language models from different companies screen the same job applications, they tend to reject the same people. We ask what these screeners share, whether it drives their decisions, and why. Seven LLM screeners from four vendors judged 800 synthetic resumes, each paired with a job description, and four of them also judged 800 real loan applications with known repayment. For each screener we estimate its template: the decision rule, not a resume layout, that links measurable features of the text to its decisions. Three findings emerge. First, all seven share one template on resumes, and its strongest ingredient is the job description's own vocabulary. Second, that ingredient is causal. Rewriting a resume to use the job description's exact terms, without changing its facts, turns rejections into selections ten times as often as the reverse. Synonyms and reformatting have no measurable effect. The LLM we used for the rewriting, told not to fabricate, added unsupported claims to 16 of the 25 rewrites that flipped a decision, and the screeners rewarded those most. Third, the template applies when there is a job description to match. On loan narratives, which have none, text features explain little of any screener's decisions, and the screeners approve between 42% and 86% of the same loans while none predicts repayment better than chance. A simple model explains the shared rule: a screener credits each requirement it recognizes, by meaning or by exact words, whichever is stronger. The model also predicts, and the data confirm, that a faithful keyword rewrite tips only resumes already close to the bar. The vendors' own technical reports show the training steps that could make that weighting common to all of them. We release a calibrated audit that needs no demographic data.
why: Real loan data audit of LLM screener templates; negative finding, transferable

title: Same Disclosure, Different Score: Country and Identity Sensitivity in AI ESG Ratings, with an Exploratory Nigeria Effect
abstract: Financial institutions are beginning to use large language models (LLMs) to read and score corporate sustainability (ESG) disclosures. We test whether such models judge identical content differently depending on the company's apparent country. In a counterfactual audit, 57 excerpts from 22 real sustainability reports were each rewritten into 13 versions that differ only in a bundle of country-associated identity cues (company name, headquarters city, stock exchange, legal suffix and nationality references): an anonymised control, six African and six Western countries. Four LLMs (Qwen3-8B, Llama 3.1 8B and Mistral 7B as 4-bit open models, and GPT-5.4 nano) scored every version, giving 13,338 scores. Our primary result is negative: pooled across models, African versions scored 0.23 points lower than Western versions on a 0–100 scale (95% CI −0.60 to +0.14), and a pilot that suggested a broader Africa penalty did not replicate. Scores were nonetheless sensitive to identity: open models shifted scores between two Western countries (UK versus France) by up to 2.5 points, and Llama 3.1 8B scored named versions 7.3 points above anonymised ones. In exploratory analysis, Nigerian versions were the lowest-scored of 12 countries for three of four models (pooled gap −1.07 points, 95% CI −1.64 to −0.53; family-wise permutation p
why: Negative result auditing LLM ESG scoring bias; evaluation discipline valuable.

title: Judge for Yourself: Confidence Beats Accuracy in AI Financial Advice
abstract: Millions now ask AI for financial advice. We study the advice they choose on Chatbot Arena, where two randomly assigned, anonymous AI models answer the same question and the user votes for the answer they prefer. Across 3,060 votes on financial questions, users select advice that is confident and actionable. The more accurate advice wins only 52.2% of decisive votes. When one answer contains a serious error while the other is factually correct, users choose the flawed answer in 47.8% of decisive votes. When an answer is verifiable, user choices favor accurate advice. The more accurate advice wins 57.6% of decisive votes when it is possible to verify the advice but only 46.9% of decisive votes if advice depends on the user's circumstances or on the future. When LLM developers train on similar preference data, they can be expected to supply more confident and less accurate advice. In our sample, we find evidence of such catering responses for Meta's Maverick model, which was tuned to perform better on Arena's leaderboard.
why: Real user votes show confidence beats accuracy in financial LLM advice.

title: Hindsight Structured Advice Distillation: Steering Executor Agents with Advisors Trained on Their Failures and Task Characteristics
abstract: Language-model agents are used for specialized work such as financial research, healthcare and law. Such agents are often capable enough for a task but still miss its details. In finance, for example, these details include which filing reports a figure or how a company discloses a metric. Retraining the agent to learn these details is expensive, and often impossible when the agent is a closed or shared system. Writing the missing know-how into the agent's prompt makes the prompt long and identical for every input, although different inputs need different guidance. We propose to learn to generate this guidance instead. A small advisor model reads each input and writes structured advice, which is appended to the prompt of a frozen executor. The advisor is trained with hindsight, following work on distillation with privileged information. On a training pool with graded answers, we analyse the executor's failures, run it under several strategies to see which one worked on each input, and let a teacher that sees the grades and the traces write the advice that would have helped. The advisor then learns, by supervised fine-tuning, to write that advice from the input alone. Because the student is a separate small model rather than the executor, it is cheap to train and adds little latency. We call this approach hindsight structured advice distillation (HSAD). On FrontierFinance, a public benchmark of expert-written financial research queries, an 8B advisor raises the qualification rate of Samaya's proprietary research agent, which already leads the benchmark's leaderboard, from 52.9% to 56.6%. This is above the agent's own high-effort configuration, at 37% lower cost per query. We study the generalization of the proposed approach, and in particular show that HSAD also improves results on WebShop, BIRD text-to-SQL and ExpertLongBench.
why: Advisor agents for finance filing tasks; agent work with finance grounding.

title: Financial YouTube Channels and the Capital Markets
abstract: This paper examines whether content creators who analyze stocks on YouTube ("Financial YouTubers") affect stock prices and liquidity. We find significant returns and increases in liquidity following video postings, with no evidence of return reversals. Retail trading primarily drives these results. Content analyses of video transcripts align directionally with the observed market reactions. We analyze the multimodal aspects of YouTube by leveraging an emotion AI tool and document that audio and video cues jointly account for 22.4% of the combined predictive contribution for returns. We find stronger market reactions for videos that produce new information, trigger more user comments-especially by younger viewers-and are released by Financial YouTubers with financial backgrounds and no channel promotional components. Finally, we find dampened market responses to videos with disclaimers. Overall, our study highlights how Financial YouTubers serve an important role in the capital markets by providing multimodal information to a growing segment of retail and younger investors. Our evidence about variation in the quality of Financial YouTuber recommendations is relevant to retail investors, professional investors, investor relations professionals, and regulators.
why: Event study of YouTube stock returns; liquidity evidence, weak AI contribution.

title: Video-based Deception Detection and Financial Fraud
abstract: Based on a comprehensive visual deception score constructed from China's mandatorily disclosed IPO roadshow videos using computer vision and machine learning, we find that visual cues embedded in these videos predict IPO financial fraud. The predictive power is incremental to financial, textual, and audio indicators. Further analyses show that these cues are well grounded in psychology research and focusing on the psychology-based deception-cue-area features improves fraud predicting performance. Furthermore, decomposing each video into five topics, we find that only the deception score of the topic on financial performance is positively associated with financial fraud. We further show that insiders of firms with higher visual deception scores are more likely to sell shares shortly after lock-up periods expire, and these firms experience significantly lower subsequent stock returns. Our study demonstrates the feasibility and potential value of using video information for fraud detection in accounting and finance.
why: Visual deception cues predict IPO fraud; single-country, incremental signal

title: Semiconductor Stock Premiums in the AI Era, 2020-2025
abstract: This paper studies the premium of large semiconductor stocks relative to the S&P 500 excluding semiconductors from 2020 to 2025. The value-weighted premium earns an FF6 alpha of 1.74% per month, while the equal-weighted premium is insignificant. Quarterly, point-in-time versions of the accounting factors of Penman and Zhang (2025) do not explain it. The premium is highly concentrated: it disappears once the two largest constituents are removed, and its increase after 2022 comes mainly from NVDA. A consensus-driven EPS growth factor built from analysts' forecasts explains about 28% of the alpha, mostly through semiconductor firms, but a significant alpha remains. Applied with the same rules to 1995-2019, the factor earns no premium. The results suggest that the AI-era semiconductor premium reflects a few mega-cap firms whose returns moved with expectations of high near-term earnings growth. Use of AI tools: AI assistants (Claude, Anthropic; Codex, OpenAI) were used to write and run code under the author’s specifications, cross-check results against the source data, and help organize and edit the text. A full statement is included in the paper.
why: Semiconductor premium factor tests; concentrated, careful but non-AI method

title: Economic Rational Structure and Distributional Risk Forecasting in Gasoline Market
abstract: Gasoline price volatility poses substantial risks for refiners, distributors, hedgers, and policymakers, yet models that perform well in point prediction need not provide equally reliable measures of conditional risk. This study uses an entropy-regularized hypergraph neural network (ERHNN) to forecast the conditional distribution of U.S. gasoline returns using weekly data from 2000 to 2025. The model combines a fixed relational representation linking crude-oil returns, crack spreads, inventories, refinery utilization, and financial conditions; a conditional Student-t predictive density; and entropy-motivated scale regularization designed to stabilize time-varying volatility. The ERHNN is evaluated against conventional volatility models, recurrent neural networks, and tree-based machine-learning benchmarks using RMSE, QLIKE, CRPS, prediction-interval coverage, and Value-at-Risk backtests. Random Forest and XGBoost achieve slightly lower RMSE, but ERHNN records the lowest CRPS and QLIKE, attains 94.7% coverage for the nominal 95% prediction interval. Neither the Kupiec nor the Dynamic Quantile tests reject the corresponding VaR calibration null for ERHNN. ERHNN records the lowest QLIKE in both high- and low-volatility states. Ablation results further show that removing the hypergraph, replacing the Student-t density with a Gaussian specification, or removing entropy regularization substantially worsens QLIKE, although restricted specifications can outperform the full model on individual point or VaR-frequency criteria. The findings therefore establish a clear distinction between point predictability and risk predictability: the model that best forecasts realized gasoline returns need not be the model that best characterizes the uncertainty surrounding those returns.
why: Hypergraph network for gasoline risk; VaR backtests, single market.

title: FOMO: FLEX Options and Market Outcomes
abstract: FLEX options are customized exchange-traded contracts allowing participants to choose nonstandard strikes, expirations, exercise styles, and settlement terms while retaining central clearing. We investigate whether single-name FLEX activity leaves measurable footprints in regular listed-option markets and underlying equities. Using a linked dataset of FLEX consolidations, daily open-interest files, listed-option chains, equity returns, and corporate actions over 250 trading days (March 2025-March 2026) across 41 underlyings and 53 event dates, we document three primary empirical findings: (1) Matched-control difference-in-differences estimates reveal a robust post-event increase in listed-option open interest (beta = 0.3061, p = 0.0042, Benjamini-Hochberg p = 0.0168). (2) FLEX activity is strongly selected into high implied-volatility (IV) environments, concentrated in mid-price underlyings (date-fixed-effect ATM IV premium beta = 0.1235, p = 0.0030). (3) Event-day IV-minus-realized-volatility spreads predict execution-stressed short-straddle returns (beta = 0.0366, p = 0.0100). Short-lived equity return effects (CAR_0 difference of -0.85%, p = 0.0442) do not persist over 1-to-5-day horizons. Overall, FLEX activity serves primarily as an observable marker of institutional volatility demand and open-interest positioning rather than a directional stock-return predictor.
why: FLEX options footprints in listed options; real data, modest method novelty.

title: MLP-Initialized Reinforcement Learning for Exit Timing in SPX Short-Straddle Portfolios
abstract: This paper studies exit timing for SPX short-straddle portfolios using a two-stage supervised and reinforcement-learning framework. Historical episodes first generate ex-post optimal hold/exit labels for training a multilayer perceptron (MLP) using only contemporaneously available state variables at deployment. The trained MLP then initializes reinforcement-learning actors that are fine-tuned with a risk-aware trading reward. Out-of-sample evaluation over 2024-2026 shows that the supervised MLP substantially outperforms passive holding and representative fixed-time and profit-and-loss-based exit rules. Across seven independent seeds, MLP-initialized Actor-Critic averages 37.54% cumulative return and a Sharpe ratio of 1.705, compared with 35.01% and 1.651 for the supervised MLP. Actor-Critic trained from scratch averages only 0.18% return. These findings show that oracle-guided supervised learning provides a stable foundation for reward-based policy fine-tuning in a sparse and path-dependent option-exit problem.
why: Supervised-then-RL SPX straddle exits; out-of-sample but limited robustness.

title: Enhancing credit risk scorecards with transactional-based behavioural features
abstract: Background: Credit risk modelling is fundamental in financial institutions, typically using credit history, repayment behaviour, income, and outstanding debt to estimate a borrower's probability of default. Although transactional data are sometimes incorporated through aggregated measures such as recency, frequency, and monetary indicators, behavioural information embedded in raw transaction narratives remains largely unexplored due to its unstructured nature. This limits opportunities to extract richer behavioural insights. Aim: This research investigates payment narratives from transactional data as an alternative data source for credit risk modelling. Setting: The study uses transactional data from a large South African financial institution focused on small and medium enterprises. Method: Techniques such as natural language processing and regular expressions are used to transform unstructured transaction descriptions into meaningful, explainable behavioural features by categorising transactions into interpretable spending categories. A novel categorisation algorithm was developed and evaluated for classification accuracy. The extracted features are incorporated into a credit risk scorecard to assess their predictive value. Results: The categorisation algorithm demonstrates high classification accuracy. Using these features in the scorecard resulted in a significant increase in Gini compared to a scorecard without them. Conclusion: Text-based transactional information can be systematically extracted, categorised, and operationalised to enhance credit risk model performance. Contribution: The study develops a novel, integrated, explainable methodology for transforming transactional text into behavioural features, introduces a structured RegEx-based categorisation approach, and demonstrates their predictive value within traditional scorecard frameworks.
why: Transaction narrative NLP for SME credit scoring; single institution

title: Realized Tail-Risk Conditional Autoregressive Expectile Models: Accurate and Stable Forecasting Performance
abstract: A realized tail-risk conditional autoregressive expectile (RTCARE) model is proposed for joint forecasting of value-at-risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES). Realized tail measures such as the realized quantile and the realized ES, constructed from intraday high-frequency returns, are incorporated into the dynamics and measurement equations of the conditional expectile, allowing information about lower-tail risk to enter the forecasts. The parameters are estimated by Markov chain Monte Carlo, and we evaluate the resulting VaR-ES forecasts in numerical examples and in an empirical application using U.S. stock-return data. Across the considered tail levels, the RTCARE models deliver competitive and often superior forecasting performance relative to existing alternatives, with stable results across Monte Carlo replications and rolling forecast evaluations.
why: Realized-measure CAViaR VaR and ES forecasts; solid econometrics, no AI

title: Evaluating Large Language Model Systems in Finance: A Claim-Centered Survey
abstract: Research on large language models (LLMs) in finance has moved from isolated tasks to systems that combine document processing, retrieval, reasoning, tool use, and human interaction. Evaluating such systems requires separating component performance from end-to-end task outcomes. Both are affected by data versions, input timing, and access constraints, so the conclusions a result supports depend on the setting in which it was obtained. This dependence has received less attention in existing surveys, which largely organize the field by model capabilities or applications. We use individual research claims, rather than whole papers or models, as the unit of analysis, because a single paper often reports several conclusions that rest on different evidence. For each claim, our E0-E5 schema characterizes the evaluation environment and clarifies which conclusions the reported evidence and boundary conditions support. Using this framework, we review the literature across four workflow stages: information acquisition and structuring, analytical reasoning, decision support, and execution, monitoring, and audit. Across these stages, the synthesis distinguishes retrieval quality from answer correctness, retrospective action evaluation from prospective testing, and model-output quality from human-reviewed task outcomes. We illustrate the framework by auditing one primary claim from each of 53 selected empirical artifacts. Building on the synthesis and audit, we derive reporting guidance that links research claims to the evidence, execution traces, and workflow conditions needed to assess them.
why: Survey of LLM-in-finance evaluation; surveys are rejected by default.

title: Reliability of Technical Stock Price Pattern Predictability
abstract: Academic research has shown throughout the years the ability of technical indicators to convey predictive value, informational content, and practical use. The popularity of such studies goes in and out over the years and today is being recognized widely by behavioral economists. Automated technical analysis is said to detect geometric and nonlinear shapes in prices which ordinary time series methods would be unable to detect. Previous papers use smoothing estimators to detect such patterns. Our paper uses local polynomial regressions, digital image processing, and state of the art machine learning tools to detect the patterns. Our results show that they are nonrandom, convey informational value, and have some predictive ability. We validate our results with prior works using stocks from the Dow Jones Industrial Average for a sample period from 1925-2019 using daily price observations.
why: Long-sample technical pattern test; reliability question, but weak method.

title: From Residuals To Returns - A Quantitative AI Approach to Stock Markets
abstract: This paper develops a mathematically rigorous framework for probabilistic market inference that operates on residuals-the idiosyncratic price movements remaining after dynamic removal of macroeconomic factors via robust Kalman filteringrather than on raw equity returns. The framework integrates five established methodological components into a unified pipeline: (i) state-space models with Student-t robust extensions for time-varying hedge coefficient estimation; (ii) a triple-validation causality gauntlet combining cross-correlation, Granger causality, and transfer entropy for nonlinear lead-lag detection; (iii) a recursive Bayesian confidence cascade of depth N , where N scales with the number of heterogeneous signal sources, computing the posterior probability that each probability estimate is wellcalibrated; (iv) Markov-switching regime detection augmented by Hurst exponent monitoring for autocorrelation structure shifts; and (v) fractional Kelly criterion position sizing derived from information-theoretic growth rate bounds, with effective probability inputs from the full Bayesian cascade. Applied to Brazilian equities (PETR4, BRFS3) using data fused from ten heterogeneous API sources-including macroeconomic indicators, commodity prices, news sentiment, weather anomalies, and social media tone—the framework reveals economically plausible lead–lag relationships invisible to standard models: VALE3 residuals lead PETR4 by +2 days (p = 0.02), corn price residuals lead BRFS3 by +3 days (p = 0.01), and Paraná rainfall anomalies lead BRFS3 by +7 days (p = 0.05). Critically, Reddit sentiment is shown to be synchronous and nonpredictive (p > 0.10), validating the framework’s capacity to reject false signals. The architecture is designed not for human discretionary trading but as a theoretical foundation for autonomous AI inference engines that must quantify, propagate, and act upon nested uncertainty. The recursive cascade structure ensures that as the variable universe expands, the system’s epistemic humility scales proportionally—more information sources produce more uncertainty layers, naturally regularizing position sizes and preventing overconfident capital allocation.
why: Kalman lead-lag pipeline; complex stack with unclear out-of-sample evidence.

title: AI-Assisted Piotroski F-score Stock Selection and Robust Portfolio Construction for Indian Equities
abstract: Indian equities offer a wide range of possibilities but come with a number of issues such as the fragmentation of the fundamentals, cyclicality of the industries, listing unevenness, portfolio-estimation error and exposures. In this study, an integrated quantamental pipeline, which consists of accounting-based fundamental screening, AI-aided industry classification, listing-adjusted price-quality filters, covariance shrinkage, blended expected-return estimation and constrained portfolio optimisation, is developed and evaluated. The pipeline begins with 752 constituents of Nifty Total Market, filters the constituents based on four criteria applicable to the sector: growth, profitability, leverage and valuation ; and uses the list of Basic Industries on the NSE to map the securities, then narrows the list to PREFERRED industries, filters using historical prices, and filters using a few more industry-specific filters: listing-history, coverage, drawdown and Sharpe-ratio. After going through the whole process, only 12 securities remain. An equal weight portfolio of the same securities, is compared with three long-only portfolios namely Global Minimum Variance (GMV), Maximum Sharpe and Blended Robust. The realised Sharpe ratios for EqualWeight, GMV, Maximum Sharpe and Blended Robust are 1.90, 1.65, 1.73 and 1.77 respectively over 2021-2026 in-sample period, whilst the benchmark has a realised Sharpe ratio of 0.33 over this same period. Blended Robust results in the highest CAGRs and EqualWeight in the best risk adjusted performance. The mean Sharpe for all seven tested rolling test folds is positive, but there is significant variation which is accompanied by at least one negative Sharpe period for each strategy. This evidence therefore provides support for the screening pipeline as a clear research and risk-governance process which does not support the argument that optimisation is better than equal weighting in terms of risk-adjusted performance. The small universe, the residual lack of look-ahead bias and the estimation uncertainty are still significant limitations.
why: India-only Piotroski pipeline; standard screens with AI labels.

title: A Distributional Framework for Behavioral Characterization and Risk Management of Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models are stochastic by nature. Repeated executions under the same experimental conditions may produce different responses. We propose a framework that can be applied across the model lifecycle, from task design to residual behavior and continuous monitoring. The method consists of building an empirical response distribution estimated through Monte Carlo simulation. Semantic interventions are introduced to study how these distributions change. We illustrate the framework with two different tasks, borrower classification and music album recommendation, and quantify the resulting distributional changes. The framework is linked to model risk management and governance by measuring robustness and control effectiveness, and characterizing residual behavior. Since it relies only on observed responses, it can also be applied to black-box models accessed through commercial APIs.
why: Distributional LLM behavior framework; borrower classification is a minor case

title: The Financing of Debt Relief: Intermediary Liquidity and the Value of Borrower Information
abstract: I study how intermediary liquidity affects mortgage resolution using 1.9 million Ginnie Mae buyout options from 2019 to 2022. When funding markets froze in 2020, nonbank issuers repurchased far fewer delinquent loans than depositories servicing loans in the same pools and, within the same issuer and month, shifted repurchases away from large balances, the loans that require the most cash. About $19 billion of repurchases were delayed, and most were completed later. A model of rationing by value per dollar of cash explains this pattern and shows that borrower information is most valuable when funding is intermediate.
why: Ginnie Mae liquidity study; real data but no AI or method transfer.

title: Does Financial Speech Need Continual Learning Regularization? A Study of EWC and mini-KFAC on Earnings Call ASR
abstract: Earnings call transcription presents a realistic continual learning scenario where Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are updated with new recordings but risk catastrophic forgetting of previously learned financial speech patterns. Adapting Whisper-small from a general-domain speech corpus to the Earnings22 benchmark reveals the opposite: all evaluated methods exhibit improvement on held-out financial speech from the same domain during adaptation rather than forgetting. This task complementarity makes regularization counterproductive. Nevertheless, when regularization is warranted, a layer-wise mini-Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (mini-KFAC) approximation seems to achieve lower word error rates (WERs) and more stable optimization than standard diagonal Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC). The results suggest that task complementarity should be assessed before applying continual learning constraints, and prefer mini-KFAC EWC over diagonal EWC when needed.
why: Earnings call ASR continual learning; finance-adjacent, narrow speech result

title: $L_0$ Feature Selection via Monte Carlo Tree Search in High-Dimensional Financial Regression
abstract: Feature selection is a central problem in high-dimensional financial regression, where large numbers of engineered variables and strong correlations among predictors reduce model stability and interpretability. $L_1$ regularization (Lasso) is widely used for sparse regression, but its shrinkage can be restrictive when informative signals are spread across correlated variables. Exact sparse regression avoids this shrinkage but requires solving a combinatorial optimization problem that is computationally difficult and is typically fit to minimize in-sample rather than out-of-sample error. This paper presents a feature selection framework based on Monte Carlo Tree Search with Generalized Nested Rollout Policy Adaptation (GNRPA). Feature selection is formulated as a sequential decision process, and candidate subsets are scored by their out-of-sample validation performance rather than training error. The method also supports a lexicographic objective accounting for subset size and multicollinearity. We study this approach on a contemporaneous explanatory regression task: explaining the weekly return of the NASDAQ-100 index from 1,072 engineered features spanning market, macroeconomic, and factor data. This isolates the value of subset selection under multicollinearity from the separate problem of predictive forecasting. On this task, the proposed method identifies sparse feature subsets with higher out-of-sample explanatory power than an optimized Lasso baseline, reaching an out-of-sample $R^2$ of 0.6961 versus 0.6313 for Lasso. These results suggest that Monte Carlo Tree Search is a practical alternative to convex regularization for sparse explanatory feature selection in financial regression, with potential value for factor attribution and risk decomposition where transparency matters as much as out-of-sample fit.
why: MCTS feature selection scored out-of-sample; evaluation-minded but niche.

title: Financial Models for Rapid AI Infrastructure Deployment
abstract: The unprecedented pace of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure deployment demands rigorous, multi-model financial evaluation frameworks capable of capturing both return potential and embedded uncertainty. This paper presents a quantitative analysis of AI infrastructure investment decisions, integrating five complementary methodologies: Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) analysis with scenario-based Net Present Value (NPV) and Internal Rate of Return (IRR), Monte Carlo simulation with 50,000 stochastic trials, Real Options Analysis (ROA) using Black-Scholes and binomial lattice models, Markowitz Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT) applied to a six-asset AI infrastructure portfolio, and Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) examining latent financial and operational drivers of deployment ROI. Empirical results indicate that base-case NPV reaches USD 1,284 million over a 10-year horizon with an IRR of 33.7%, substantially exceeding a 10% WACC hurdle rate. Monte Carlo analysis yields a median NPV of USD 2,424 million with P(NPV > 0) = 99.9%, confirming strong investment viability. Real options modelling reveals significant option premia under high volatility conditions (σ = 50-65%), underscoring the strategic value of staged deployment. Portfolio optimisation identifies a maximum Sharpe ratio of 0.75, with cloud AI platforms and data storage receiving dominant allocations (33.7% and 21.6%, respectively). SEM path analysis confirms that financial capacity exerts the strongest direct effect on deployment speed (β = 0.62, p
why: Generic DCF, Monte Carlo and MPT framing; AI is only a label

title: Is the Business of Frontier AI Companies Selling Tokens? Value Capture and Equity Prices
abstract: We examine business models that could support frontier AI companies' valuations and the public evidence of plans to earn income beyond selling model access. Treating the announced financing prices as hypothetical operating-value targets, reverse cash-flow calculations for OpenAI and Anthropic yield combined year-ten revenue requirements of $2.79 trillion or $733 billion, depending on financial assumptions. Public documents identify proposed payments and ownership interests that could supply additional income, such as through partnerships on pharmaceuticals, robotics, or materials science. We discuss how these arrangements relate to firm boundaries and value capture.
why: Valuation back-of-envelope on AI firms; commentary, not evidence.

title: Support Vector Machines for Financial Classification: From IBEX-35 Forecasting to Probabilistic Classification and a Novel Two-class Framework
abstract: Technical analysis and machine learning offer complementary approaches to the classification of financial market behavior. Traditional technical analysis relies on the identification of recurring price patterns, while machine learning provides methods for transforming observed market information into representations that can be evaluated systematically. This paper reviews the application of support vector machines (SVMs) to financial classification, connecting prior research on stock-market forecasting and technical-pattern recognition with a proposed image-based, two-class classification framework. The discussion considers the role of SVM decision boundaries, kernel functions, and probabilistic calibration, including Platt scaling, in distinguishing between alternative market outcomes. It also considers the use of numerical price-pattern detection and chart-image representations as alternative approaches to encoding market information. The proposed framework treats visual price patterns as structured inputs whose pixel values or derived features may be used to train a binary classifier. An illustrative two-class example and Mathematica-based computational materials provide a foundation for describing the methodology. The framework is intended to support reproducible investigation of whether image-derived representations contain useful classification information beyond conventional technical indicators. Its predictive effectiveness, generalizability, and practical investment value require empirical testing using chronological out-of-sample evaluation, appropriate benchmarks, and controls for look-ahead bias and transaction costs.
why: SVM review with proposed image framework; no convincing evidence visible.

title: Do Earnings Announcements Cause Power Outages? The Externality of Machine-based Information Processing for Local Power System Reliability
abstract: Capital market participants increasingly use machine-based information technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), to process information. As a key component of the infrastructure supporting these technologies, data centers require substantial electricity inputs. Using daily variation in concurrent earnings announcements (EAs) to capture spikes in the volume of capital market information, we examine whether machine-based information processing creates a negative externality for local power-system reliability. We find that, on days with more concurrent EAs, counties with greater exposure to data centers experience significantly more power outages. The effect is stronger when daily EAs exhibit characteristics associated with greater demand for information processing, including larger average absolute earnings surprises and a higher percentage of firms announcing losses. The effect is also stronger when a greater percentage of EAs are bundled with same-day 10-K or 10-Q filings and when these same-day filings are longer and less readable. Finally, the effect becomes stronger after the release of ChatGPT for counties with greater exposure to hyperscale data centers, which are more likely to support generative AI and large language model workloads. Overall, by documenting a previously overlooked cost of capital-market technologies borne by parties outside the capital markets, we document broader welfare implications of technological advances in capital markets.
why: Earnings announcements and outages; tangential to trading or ML practice.

title: Regression Analysis on the Modifications of Fama and French Five Factor Model applied to Philippine Common Stocks from 2013-2020
abstract: Multi-factor models have been used to determine the explanatory power of certain economic factors on stock return variations in the market. In this study, modifications of the Fama and French five-factor model, including the six-factor model, are applied to Philippine common stock returns from 2013 to 2020. Multiple linear regression via ordinary least squares (OLS) is implemented to estimate the parameters of the models. The six-factor model (6FM) emerged as the most robust, improving explanatory power for 15 out of 16 portfolios, further revealing significant relationships between the factors. Support vector regression (SVR) is then applied to 6FM to determine the relationship between the independent and dependent variables. Results show that SVR with radial basis kernel function (RBF) achieved competitive results after hyperparameter optimization. Analysis and results highlight the utility of combining traditional regression methods with advanced machine learning techniques to enhance model accuracy in portfolio analysis.
why: Philippine factor-model regressions; single-country, no new method.

title: Realism VS Accuracy: Event Sequence Forecasting from a Generative Modeling Perspective
abstract: Event sequences are chains of random events, each described by heterogeneous (numerical and categorical) features. The problem of event sequence forecasting occurs in finance, healthcare, business process intelligence, and other fields. In this work, we study multi-horizon forecasting of event sequences as a conditional generative modeling problem. We evaluate forecasts not only for prediction accuracy, but also for distributional realism. To this end, we present a benchmark comprising metrics for both quality aspects, strong statistical baselines, recent models adapted from adjacent fields, and curated real-world datasets. Careful evaluation reveals that no method excels at both accuracy and realism, highlighting a fundamental trade-off between the two. Finally, we introduce Wasserstein BaryBooster, an algorithm that aggregates samples from a realism-strong diffusion model into a state-of-the-art predictor, demonstrating that distributional realism can be converted into prediction accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/xaosina/event-sequence-forecasting.
why: Generic event-sequence generative benchmark; finance is incidental.

title: Restricted Entropic and Quadratic Hedging in the Small-Risk-Aversion Limit
abstract: In incomplete markets, contingent claims cannot in general be replicated exactly, and hedging must therefore be formulated as an optimization problem over admissible trading strategies. This paper studies the relation between quadratic hedging and entropic hedging in a discrete-time incomplete market when strategies are restricted to bounded finite-dimensional parametric classes. These restrictions induce admissible gain sets that are compact and convex in \(L^2\), providing a common well-posed setting for both the restricted mean-square hedging problem and the restricted exponential-utility hedging problem. The main contribution is to establish a uniform small-risk-aversion expansion of the entropic risk functional over the restricted gain set and to use this uniformity to obtain convergence of the corresponding minimizers. Under a uniform exponential integrability assumption, the restricted entropic hedging gains converge in \(L^2\) to the unique restricted quadratic hedge as the risk-aversion parameter tends to zero. The theoretical result is illustrated numerically in a regularized discrete-time stochastic volatility model of Heston type.
why: Hedging theory in small-risk-aversion limit; no data or implementation.

title: Entropy Regularization under No-Shorting: Structure Preservation and Convexity in Dynamic Mean-Variance Portfolio Selection
abstract: This paper studies entropy regularization for the discrete-time dynamic mean--variance portfolio problem with no-shorting constraints. In the unconstrained setting, entropy regularization can be introduced without changing the basic quadratic structure of the dynamic program. Under no-shorting, this property is lost: a standard fixed-temperature formulation generally preserves convexity but no longer preserves the homogeneous Bellman structure and the associated piecewise-linear feedback form. We introduce a state-dependent temperature that is matched to the homogeneity of the original mean--variance problem. This restores the piecewise-quadratic value function and the finite-dimensional Bellman recursion. The resulting formulation, however, makes convexity depend on the continuation coefficients generated by the soft recursion. We show that negative continuation coefficients lead to loss of convexity and prove that a common sufficiently small temperature preserves the Bellman structure and convexity over the entire finite horizon. The original no-shorting solution is recovered as the temperature vanishes. We also develop a sample-based implementation for unknown return distributions. Numerical and empirical results illustrate both the structural advantage of the state-dependent temperature and the practical relevance of the convexity-preserving temperature restriction.
why: Entropy-regularized mean-variance theory; no data or implementation path.

title: Three options are roughly enough - Variance-optimal semi-static hedging in the rough Heston model
abstract: This paper studies semi-static variance-optimal hedging of variance swaps in the rough Heston model under a risk-neutral measure. We combine dynamic trading in the underlying asset with static positions in a finite basket of European options, with the aim of minimizing the variance of the residual hedging error. Exploiting the Markovian lift provided by the forward variance curve, the Fourier representations of the claims and the Laplace transform characterization of the log-price, we derive semi-explicit formulas for the optimal strategies and the hedging error. We then study the optimal claim selection problem, investigating numerically how the choice of static instruments depends on the Hurst index. Under standard parametrization, we discover that "three options are roughly enough", i.e. adding three static vanilla options reduces the hedging error by more than 95% relative to the purely dynamic hedge for all considered roughness regimes H= 0.1, 0.3, 0.5.
why: Rough Heston variance hedging theory; numerical, no practitioner data.

title: CorrFlow: Exact and Permutation-Equivariant Flow Matching on the Correlation Elliptope
abstract: Correlation matrices combine nonlinear positive-definiteness constraints with a simultaneous row-column permutation symmetry. Their generation therefore involves two distinct problems. First, every output must remain on the correlation elliptope, irrespective of how its variables are ordered. Second, the generator must learn the domain-specific distribution occupied by empirical data inside that valid space. Existing financial image generators mix these problems: they learn ordered matrix entries and repair invalid draws afterward. We introduce CorrFlow, which separates them. A generalized Fisher transform maps full-rank correlation matrices bijectively to unconstrained coordinates, guaranteeing valid outputs without projection. A graph flow-matching network learns the empirical distribution in those coordinates and is permutation equivariant: reordering the variables only reorders the output. We compare a conditional CorrGAN reimplementation, image diffusion, and CorrFlow on $80\times80$ Taiwan equity matrices using five seeds per neural method. CorrFlow produces 100% valid draws without repair and obtains feature sliced-Wasserstein distance $.712\pm.141$, versus $4.339\pm.252$ for CorrGAN and $4.610\pm.191$ for image diffusion after their invalid outputs are projected back to the correlation space. It also improves this distance over historical lookup, while lookup retains higher local coverage. These results support the combined construction under the evaluated training budget; they do not establish superiority over fully tuned image models or isolate the contribution of each component.
why: Correlation matrix generative flow model; limited finance application visible.

title: Supply Chain Finance, Redefined: What Fifteen Years of Research Have Taught Operations, Finance, Accounting and Economics, and Where the Field Should Go Next
abstract: Supply chain finance is usually defined as a product: early payment of supplier invoices against the buyer's credit. Pandemic liquidity shocks, supply chain reconfiguration, tariffs and sanctions have shown that financing works through prices, payment terms and risk allocations between firms. I argue for a broader definition. Supply chain finance is the set of operating, financial and risk management decisions that determine who holds working capital, who holds risk, and at what price. Three shifts follow. Decisions are joint, because financing terms move prices and quantities. Prices absorb subsidies, because relief granted to one firm is partly captured by its counterparty through the price. Risk moves, it does not vanish; hedges, guarantees and payment extensions relocate it. My work with coauthors yields ten propositions. Trade credit priced below fair value is a volume instrument recovered through the wholesale price. Non-recourse factoring does not dominate recourse, and an optimized reverse factoring program need not extend payment terms. A loan guarantee is partly captured upstream through a higher input price, can raise default among the weakest borrowers, and turns the credit spread into a report on coverage. Buy now pay later raises volume almost mechanically but profit only when the effective price clears the merchant's margin requirement, and cash-paying customers subsidize it. A risk-neutral firm should hedge cash flow to protect its investment program, and its partner's hedging decision matters. Financial hedges suit transactional exposure; operational and competitive exposures call for operational and financial hedges together. Revenue sharing coordinates under default because the wholesale price reallocates channel debt, and contracts facing volatile inputs must be indexed and penalized. Fifteen years of work by others in operations, finance, economics and accounting has confirmed the joint decision premise, the investment rationale for hedging and the transmission of financial shocks along chains, while contesting the direction of risk shifting in trade credit, the value of buyer-led programs to suppliers, and the safety effect of guarantees. The next decade should model multi-tier chains, separate risk that moves from risk that vanishes, study nonbank lenders, climate and geopolitical risk and artificial intelligence, and measure operational hedges.
why: Position-style review of supply chain finance; no practitioner method.

title: Automating the Broken: Bridging the AI Actuator Gap Through Pipeline Circuit Breakers and Systemic Risk Stewardship
abstract: During the acceleration of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption across highly regulated sectors, enterprises face a critical governance vulnerability: the Actuator Gap. Traditional IT governance models rely on static perimeters; however, autonomous agentic systems execute tasks across multi-cloud environments at machine speed, transforming flawed legacy processes into immediate, kinetic operational liabilities. While telemetry and post-hoc audit logging provide necessary visibility, detection without automated intervention is insufficient to halt unauthorized machine execution. This article presents a dual-pillar governance architecture that operationalizes the People, Process, and Technology (PPT) imperative. Grounded in the ISO/IEC 38500 Evaluate-Direct-Monitor (EDM) model and ISO/IEC 42001, the proposed framework introduces pipeline-native technical circuit breakers—utilizing Governance as Code (GaC), automated promotion gates, and real-time observability—to deterministically halt policy-violating agents. Concurrently, this model addresses the leadership bottleneck through Systemic Risk Stewardship, redefining C-suite accountability from tactical task proximity to intentional decision-boundary design as mandated by ISO/IEC 38500. Fusing deterministic technical controls with executive accountability allows organizations to safely scale autonomous systems without forfeiting enterprise governance integrity.
why: AI governance architecture; off-topic for financial ML practice.

title: Optimizing Credit Card Fraud Detection through a Hybridized ANN-Non-linear SVM Ensemble: A Comparative Analysis with Gradient Boosting and Linear Classifiers
abstract: Credit card fraud remains a major challenge in the digital financial sector, creating substantial risks for both financial institutions and consumers. This study presents a hybrid machine learning approach for detecting fraudulent credit card transactions by combining an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) with a nonlinear Support Vector Machine (SVM). The study also addresses the challenge of highly imbalanced transaction data by considering oversampling techniques and cost-sensitive learning. The dataset was obtained from Kaggle and contains 284,807 credit card transactions, including 492 fraudulent and 284,315 legitimate transactions. The data were divided into training and testing sets using a 70:30 split. The proposed hybrid approach combines the pattern-learning capability of the ANN with the nonlinear classification and generalization ability of the SVM. Experimental results show that the standalone ANN achieved a precision of 0.88, recall of 0.71, F1score of 0.78, and accuracy of 0.99. The linear SVM produced comparatively weaker results, while the nonlinear SVM provided a more balanced performance. The proposed hybrid model achieved a precision of 0.89, recall of 0.75, F1-score of 0.81, accuracy of 0.99, and an AUC-ROC of 0.94. Compared with the individual models, the hybrid approach produced noticeable improvements in recall and F1-score, indicating better identification of fraudulent transactions while maintaining high overall accuracy. The findings demonstrate the potential of combining complementary machine learning models to improve credit card fraud detection, particularly in highly imbalanced datasets. The proposed approach provides a practical foundation for developing more reliable fraud detection systems. Future work will investigate real-time deployment and the use of temporal modelling techniques to capture changing fraud patterns and improve detection of emerging forms of fraudulent activity.
why: Kaggle fraud classifier comparison; toy benchmark, no finance depth.

title: Regulating Artificial Intelligence in Finance: Lessons from Singapore
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the global financial sector, with widespread adoption across banking, insurance, and other financial services. Singapore exemplifies this trend. Its major financial institutions, including DBS, OCBC, and UOB, have extensively integrated AI and Generative AI (GenAI) to enhance efficiency, productivity, and customer experience. However, the growing use of AI in finance also introduces significant risks related to transparency, data privacy, cybersecurity, fairness, accountability, GenAI hallucinations, and deepfakes. This paper examines Singapore's regulatory approach to governing AI in finance, anchored by the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) multi-layered strategy that combines principles-based regulation, collaborative industry engagement, supervisory technology (SupTech) adoption, market-enabling measures, and deliberate regulatory gradualism. While Singapore's framework, comprising the FEAT Principles, Project MindForge, and the MAS Guidelines on AI Risk Management, provides a strong foundation, this paper suggests areas for improvement. These include elevating guidelines into enforceable codes, addressing third-party AI risks, leveraging SupTech capabilities, establishing a dedicated AI regulatory sandbox, and ensuring robust enforcement and international cooperation. Drawing lessons from Singapore's experience, this paper argues that effective AI governance in finance requires not a singular approach but a calibrated, adaptive combination of strategies suited to each jurisdiction's institutional context and evolving technological landscape. Ultimately, responsible AI governance demands a multi-layered regulatory ecosystem, and the institutional capacity to evolve alongside the technology it seeks to govern.
why: Regulatory description of Singapore AI policy; no transferable method.

title: Insulating Agricultural Credit Portfolios Against Climate Shocks: An Econometric Probit and Machine Learning Analysis of Credit-tied Weather Index Microinsurance Author: Isaac Nketsiah
abstract: The exposure of smallholder farmers to crop losses, fluctuation of income and difficulties in getting credit to finance their farming practices have all intensified with time, as a result of climate shocks. The risks can be more widespread than the farm household they affect, and can impact financial institutions with a high concentration of agricultural loans that are at risk of loss if residents are unable to repay. One possible solution to such risks is to insure against them based on the credit and lines of production in the agricultural sector and automatically be paid out when some weather conditions like low rainfall or floods are experienced beyond a predetermined threshold. However, there can be neutralization of these structures by basis risk, financial attributes of the household and borrower differentiated climate and repayment riskiness. The paper discusses the possibility to avert agricultural credit risk where exposed to climate change by credit-linked weather-index microinsurance, and how it is plausible to use econometric and machine-learning tools to filter out susceptible borrowers to insurance and repayment risk. The empirical analysis is an amalgamation of household attributes, which pertain to agriculture and microinsurance and climate and weather, financial and transactional conditions, and basis risk. The probability of a relevant outcome of credit or insurance risk and the marginal effects of these outcomes are calculated using a Probit regression model. A parallel machine-learning classification model is built which then categorizes borrowers under perceived risk profiles and measures the performance of the model. Comparisons manifold: the statistical inference and predictive performance are compared using sufficient measures, including the measures of classification accuracy and precision, recall and F1-score, ROC-AUC among other measure performance-relevant measures. Following the empirical analysis of the data set, facts about coefficients, marginal effects and forecast outcomes will be reported. The lessons rely on the findings and are aimed to provide evidence of how the insurance and credit functions could be combined to enable climate-risk management of ag finance to smallholder.
why: Agricultural microinsurance probit study; off-topic for this reader.

title: Auditable Data Pipelines for AI-Based Spear-Phishing Detection in Financial Cybersecurity: A Systematic Review of Data Quality and Blockchain Foundations
abstract: Ensuring the integrity, provenance, and auditability of the data on which security systems depend is a central challenge in financial cybersecurity, and one to which blockchain and distributed-ledger technologies are increasingly applied. AI-based threat detectors are only as trustworthy as the logs and training data they consume, yet those data are rarely tamper-evident or verifiable. Spear-phishing, a leading intrusion vector into financial institutions, is used throughout as the motivating application case. This paper examines how data quality and blockchain-enabled auditability jointly condition AI-driven threat detection in the financial sector, through a PRISMA 2020 systematic review of research published between 2020 and 2025. Searches across Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library retrieved 250 records, of which 202 remained after deduplication and 59 met the eligibility and quality-appraisal criteria after a full bibliographic verification of publication dates. The review consolidates four literatures that have developed in parallel, namely blockchain-enabled auditability, data quality, AI-based detection, and financial cybersecurity, and derives a thematic taxonomy of how each treats log integrity, provenance, and data governance. It diagnoses a bounded structural gap: blockchain studies establish immutability and provenance but do not integrate them into operational detection pipelines, whereas AI-detection studies treat data auditability as an implicit assumption. Building on this, the article specifies an auditable Logging–Blockchain–AI (LBA) pipeline through five design requirements (R1–R5) covering ledger interoperability with heterogeneous logging infrastructure, on-ledger governance aligned with financial regulation, data-quality and drift monitoring, scalability, and explainability with human oversight. A bounded scope statement is made explicit: within the reviewed corpus, only six studies treat spear-phishing as their primary research problem, so the review characterises the data-quality and auditability foundations on which such detection depends rather than the detection literature itself. The contribution is analytical and agenda-setting.
why: Systematic review of cybersecurity data pipelines; off-topic.

title: DeFiRank: Federated Pairwise Ranking for Governance in Decentralized Financial Networks
abstract: Existing governance approaches in decentralized financial networks rely on manual review processes conducted by human committees, which introduces subjective bias, creates a scalability bottleneck under high network volume, and fails to capture complex behavioural patterns and evolving network dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose \name, a federated learning-based pairwise ranking framework in which multiple institutions collaboratively train a ranking model without sharing their private transaction data. This collaborative learning enables the model to capture network-wide behavioural patterns that signify strong network participation and directly contribute to the network effect, including diversity of counterparties, usage of multiple applications, and frequency of transactions. The proposed system ranks providers based on the authenticity of their actions, promoting genuine contributors and demoting those exhibiting suspicious behaviour. We evaluate \name\ on a real-world blockchain transaction dataset. Results demonstrate that the federated approach achieves ranking performance modestly below the centralized baseline (NDCG@15: $\approx$0.87 vs.\ $\approx$0.92) while preserving data privacy and matching its ranking stability (Kendall $τ$: $\approx$0.70 for both regimes), producing reliable governance decisions, including provider promotion and demotion (648 and 39 unique providers, respectively), without requiring centralized access to sensitive transaction data.
why: Federated governance ranking for DeFi providers; off-topic for finance research.

title: DAG Structure Learning with Node-Varying Heavy-Tailed Disturbances
abstract: DAG structures can be learned from observations by incorporating acyclicity via smooth constraints, such as DAGMA's log-determinant function. Typically, observations and the underlying DAG are related through linear structural equation models, with Gaussianity assumption on the disturbances at each node. Extending DAG learning methods that account for scale and tail behavior of disturbances that vary across nodes remains a challenge. We propose a node-varying Student-$t$ DAGMA that jointly estimates the graph structure, node-specific disturbance scales, and the degrees-of-freedom parameter. A Gaussian scale-mixture representation yields an iteratively reweighted formulation that down-weights large standardized residuals. Building on existing results, we also establish identifiability of the graph and disturbance parameters. Synthetic experiments demonstrate improved structural recovery under heterogeneous heavy-tailed disturbances, and experiments on real finance data show that the proposed method yields lower test negative log-likelihood than the evaluated baselines.
why: DAG structure learning theory; no finance content.

title: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data
abstract: Selecting a subset of features (columns) from a tabular dataset is a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications. Industry experts seek to minimize model training costs, climate scientists require an interpretable subset of factors to understand extreme weather events, and clinicians need to choose among diagnostic tests due to financial and time constraints. When looking at the scientific literature to determine which feature selection method to use, practitioners across domains face an unrepresentative landscape of benchmarking. Despite extensive research, existing feature selection benchmarks provide limited guidance because they rely on outdated models, ad hoc evaluation protocols, or artificially generated data that do not reflect real-world problems. To close the gap between scientific benchmarking and real-world applications, we introduce SelectArena, a modern benchmark for feature selection. We compare 15 widely used feature selection methods on 71 manually curated real-world tabular datasets, covering classification and regression problems, using standardized evaluation protocols and state-of-the-art tabular (foundation) models. Our results reveal clear trade-offs across predictive performance, runtime, stability, and validity. Tree-based methods, CART and RFImportance, along with F-Test are Pareto-optimal when taking into account predictive performance and runtime. F-Test, information-theory-, and distance-based methods lead on stability and validity, with F-Test emerging as a balanced choice across our metrics. Search-based methods are slow, unstable and achieve low performance. SelectArena turns these findings into practical guidance and, as an extensible platform, supports future feature selection research.
why: General tabular feature selection benchmark; not finance-specific.

title: Human Knowledge Capital and the Watt Standard: A Framework for Making the Invisible Inputs of the Advanced Intelligence Economy Visible
abstract: Advanced Intelligence depends on two inputs whose contributions are recognised in many contexts but are not consistently connected to the AI services they enable. Collective knowledge is supported by public research, education, scientific infrastructure and intellectual property, yet a common framework for describing the collective knowledge foundation of a particular service remains insufficiently developed. Electricity is metered, certified and reported for facilities and organisations, yet it is not consistently disclosed at the level of a defined AI service. This paper describes the resulting challenge as an accounting gap in the Advanced Intelligence economy. Building on the WAIA White Paper, this paper develops two instruments. Human Knowledge Capital is an analytical category for collective knowledge contributions, refined through a four-layer taxonomy and the concepts of Unattributed Capital and Knowledge Rent. The Watt Standard is a proposed service-level reporting framework that brings together physical electricity consumption, energy-procurement claims and per-service electricity intensity for a defined AI service. The extent to which existing instruments provide these elements in one integrated service-level disclosure remains to be established through systematic comparison with relevant literature, technical standards and reporting practices. The proposed framework's added value must be tested through that comparison and a pilot study. The paper contributes a reporting template—the Watt Record—a staged implementation pathway and a set of testable research questions. It does not claim that collective knowledge has a single measurable price, that energy use measures the value of knowledge, or that recognising a contribution automatically justifies collecting revenue.
why: Accounting framework essay on AI inputs; content-free for this reader.

title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, and Risk Governance for Trustworthy Digital Financial Reporting: A Conceptual Framework
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain are transforming financial reporting through automated transaction processing, digital asset reconciliation, data verification, and enhanced auditability. However, their integration presents challenges involving data integrity, cybersecurity, algorithmic accountability, regulatory compliance, and organizational coordination. Implementing these technologies independently may create fragmented controls and unreliable reporting outcomes. This article develops a conceptual framework integrating AIenabled financial reporting, blockchain-based transaction verification, zero-trust cybersecurity, and organizational risk governance. Drawing on literature on digital asset accounting, trustworthy AI, enterprise risk management, and information security, the framework identifies five interconnected dimensions: data provenance and integrity, intelligent transaction processing, blockchain-enabled traceability, risk-based security and governance, and continuous organizational feedback. Eight propositions are developed to guide future empirical investigation, supported by three tables outlining the framework, propositions, and implementation priorities. The article argues that trustworthy digital financial reporting depends on accurate source data, explainable automated decisions, verifiable transaction records, proportionate security controls, and clearly defined accountability. The study contributes to accounting and information systems research by conceptualizing digital financial reporting as a governed socio-technical process in which technological reliability and organizational oversight jointly influence reporting quality. Practical recommendations include establishing data ownership, validating AI outputs, maintaining traceable reconciliation records, enforcing leastprivilege access controls, and assessing reporting accuracy, completeness, timeliness, and auditability. The framework provides a foundation for investigating how integrated digital governance enhances reporting reliability, organizational resilience, and stakeholder trust.
why: Conceptual AI-blockchain reporting framework; no data or implementation path.

title: Bridging Digital Twins and Life-Cycle-Aware Dispatch of Power-to-X Assets: ACritical Perspective for Grid Flexibility
abstract: Power-to-X (P2X) assets can enhance grid flexibility by coupling variable electricity supply with hydrogen, gas, chemical, heating, and cooling networks. However, frequent grid-responsive operation may accelerate asset degradation and challenge multiphysics safety boundaries of capital-intensive P2X assets. From a critical perspective of grid flexibility, this paper elucidates a conceptual life-cycle-aware dispatch paradigm, and subsequently develops a digital-twin-to-dispatch (DT-to-dispatch) framework for bridging DTs with life-cycleaware dispatch. Building on advances in DTs and physics-informed AI, the proposed DT-to-dispatch frameworktranslates synchronized asset-health states into dynamic flexibility envelopes and life-cycle-aware marginal costs, enabling dispatch decisions to balance short-term economic returns while accounting for long-term asset service-life expenses. Evidence is organized across four enabling functions: DT synchronization, virtual sensing, surrogate modeling, and cyber-trust. The direct evidence of DT-to-dispatch technology has been found in power-to-hydrogen applications but limited and transferable evidence of use for other P2X applications, suchas power-to-gas, power-to-heat/cooling, and power-to-chemicals. Accordingly, the proposed DT-to-dispatch is a research and validation framework rather than an already demonstrated generic solution. Future research should prioritize integrating DT-to-dispatch frameworks into an energy management system (EMS) for developing scalable, secure, trustworthy, and economically life-cycle-aware P2X dispatch solutions.
why: Power-to-X dispatch conceptual framework; off-topic for finance.

title: MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis
abstract: Data-centric scaling of RLVR has focused on collecting or generating verifiable training problems. However, corpus size alone does not determine whether the dataset provides a useful learning signal for a target policy. To guide the synthesis of effective RLVR data, we experimentally characterize dataset effectiveness as a function of its problems, the target policy, and the training rollout budget. Under this characterization, we show that a large open-source math corpus pooled from widely used RLVR datasets falls almost entirely into a zero-advantage trap: for a fixed target policy and rollout budget, roughly 88% of its problems are solved in every rollout or failed in every rollout. Filtering concentrates what remains, but it can only select, discarding the hard problems. Effective synthetic problems should therefore require the reasoning operations and compositions required to solve those hard problems. Yet their difficulty must be calibrated, so that some rollouts succeed, some fail, and at least one correct solution fits within the training budget. Prompting a teacher to vary hard problems directly does not achieve this. Guided by these empirical principles, we introduce MagicBeanStalk, a top-down decomposition and bottom-up recursive data-synthesis algorithm that grows seed problems into families of substantively new, policy- and budget-calibrated training problems while preserving the seeds' reasoning blueprints. Across 8 math benchmarks, continual RLVR on MagicBeanStalk problems improves gpt-oss-120b from 61.2 to 69.8 (+8.6) and DeepSeek v4Flash from 72.4 to 77.9 (+5.4) on a 16K-token budget. Training on the full 78K source corpus improves by only +1.1 and its best filtered real data subset by +5.8. In finance, we synthesize over 14K verifiable problems from only 340 solutions and improve over base by 6.9 and 2.4 points on SecQue and FinanceBench, respectively.
why: RLVR math data synthesis; no finance content

title: Machine Unlearning for Federated Socially Fair k-Means Clustering
abstract: Federated clustering can support applications such as patient stratification across hospitals and customer segmentation across distributed financial datasets. Responsible AI calls for fair representation of demographic groups and support for data deletion, motivated in part by rights such as the GDPR's right to erasure. These goals interact: deleting records can change the balance between groups and alter the clustering of the remaining population. We study exact machine unlearning for federated socially fair $k$-means, whose objective is to minimize the largest group-average squared distance to the nearest center. Our approach keeps separate local summaries for each group, so summaries at unaffected institutions remain valid as global fairness weights change. For two groups, we prove an initialization approximation guarantee independent of client group proportions under ideal sampling, and we show that same-seed replay reproduces retraining exactly. Reuse pays off most when a whole client withdraws: across three datasets, replay is $35.8\times$ faster than retraining for the initialization-only model and remains $2.4\times$ and $1.7\times$ faster with one and two fair-refinement rounds, which improve worst-group cost. For individual record deletions, gains are modest (about $1.06\times$), and certifying cached assignments can cost more than it saves. These results map where exact unlearning can profitably reuse computation. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/arareddy/mufsc.
why: Federated k-means unlearning; no finance content visible.
